summary: Three towers on Monte Titano and a walled hilltop capital looking out to the Adriatic.
overview: San Marino calls itself the world's oldest surviving republic, founded, so the story goes, in 301 by Marinus, a stonemason who took refuge on the mountain. It covers about 61 km² of hills entirely surrounded by Italy, a short way inland from Rimini. The capital, the Città di San Marino, runs along the ridge of Monte Titano, about 740 m high, with cliffs on one side and three towers, Guaita, Cesta and Montale, strung out along the top. A path joins the first two, and on clear days the view runs across Romagna to the Adriatic. The old centre and the mountain are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Inside the walls, steep lanes lead up to the Palazzo Pubblico, where the Great and General Council meets and the Guard of the Rock stands outside in green and red; the Basilica of San Marino holds the saint's relics. Below the ridge, Borgo Maggiore has an old market square and a cable car up to the capital. There's no airport or railway: most visitors come by bus from Rimini or by car, and the day-trippers leave by late afternoon, so staying the night means quiet streets and floodlit towers. Two Captains Regent, elected every six months, share the role of head of state.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.text: Cold and often misty on the summit, with days around 5–8°C, frost, and snow in some years. Quiet, with Christmas lights and stalls in the old town in December.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.text: Often clear and mild, good for long views. The new Captains Regent take office in ceremony on 1 April, and May is warm and green.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.text: Warm but breezier than the coast, with days of 26–28°C. Coaches from the Rimini beach resorts fill the lanes in July and August, and the Medieval Days bring crossbows and costumes.

seasons.name: Autumn
seasons.text: Clear, warm days carry on through September, and the national day falls on the 3rd. Rain comes more often in October and November, when cloud can hide the view.

whenToGo.weather: Monte Titano rises straight out of the hills behind the Adriatic coast, so the capital is a few degrees cooler and windier than the beaches. Summer days usually reach 26–28°C; winter days are around 5–8°C, nights hover near freezing, and snow falls in some years. Rain, roughly 800 mm a year, comes in every season, most of all in autumn, and low cloud sometimes wraps the summit.

festivals.name: Feast of St Agatha
festivals.text: The republic's co-patron saint has her feast on the day in 1740 when an occupation by the papal legate, Cardinal Alberoni, came to an end; shops and offices close.

festivals.name: Investiture of the Captains Regent
festivals.text: The two new heads of state, chosen for six months, are sworn in, with a procession of officials and guards in ceremonial dress through the old town.

festivals.name: Medieval Days (Giornate Medioevali)
festivals.when: Usually in late July, over a few days
festivals.text: The old town goes back in time with crossbow contests, flag throwers, craft markets, music and food from old recipes.

festivals.name: Feast of San Marino and the Founding of the Republic
festivals.text: San Marino's own day, for the saint and the founding of the republic in 301, with ceremonies at the basilica and a contest of the republic's crossbowmen.

culture.greetings: Manners are much as in Italy: a handshake on meeting, “Buongiorno” until mid-afternoon and “Buonasera” after, and two kisses on the cheeks among friends. The Sammarinese are proud of their long independence, and like visitors to treat San Marino as a country of its own rather than a corner of Italy.
etiquette: For a souvenir, the tourist office will stamp your passport with San Marino's own stamp, for a small fee.
Cover your shoulders and knees in the basilica and the churches.
The paths between the towers run along cliff edges: keep to them, and wear shoes with grip, as the stone is slippery after rain.
The old town is largely closed to traffic, so park in the car parks below the walls and walk up.
culture.tipping: As in Italy, bills often include a small cover charge (coperto), and tips aren't expected. Rounding up, or leaving a few euros for good service, is welcome.
culture.dress: Comfortable shoes for steep cobbles and steps, and an extra layer: the summit is windier and cooler than the beaches below.

food.name: Torta Tre Monti
food.text: Layers of thin wafer and hazelnut and chocolate cream, coated in chocolate, with the three towers on top. Sold in boxes all over town.

food.name: Piadina
food.text: The flatbread of Romagna, folded round prosciutto, soft squacquerone cheese and rocket, or torn and eaten with a meal.

food.name: Passatelli
food.text: Short, thick strands of breadcrumbs, Parmesan, egg and nutmeg pressed straight into hot broth, a winter favourite here and across Romagna.

food.name: Sangiovese and Biancale
food.text: Wines from the republic's own vineyards: red Sangiovese and whites such as Biancale, sold in shops and at the cooperative cellar.

phrases.intro: Italian is the language of everyday life, and older people also speak Romagnol, the dialect of the surrounding region. English is common in the old town's shops.

items.text: Euro (€). San Marino isn't in the EU, but it mints its own euro coins, mostly sold to collectors.
